headline: Wamphassuc rocks go quiet at noon, loud at midnight: eel bite on and fluke picking up the slack
subhead: A soft neap tide is stretching the striper window into the dark hours while fluke and sea bass carry the boulder fields through the day.
body_markdown:
First light off Ram Island and the bait tells you everything before you make a cast. Peanut bunker pinned tight against the rocks, silversides skittering along the boulder faces where the current still has some shape to it, terns working low and quick. By nine o'clock the wind lays down, the sun gets on the water, and it all goes still. That's the tell this time of year — the bait isn't gone, it's just gone quiet, and so are the fish that were pushing it.

Water's running warm through here. New London's reading 69.4, and up toward the western Sound Kings Point is pushing 70.9. That's enough heat in the shallows to shove the bass into a nighttime pattern, and I'm seeing it in my own water — the boulder fields off Wamphassuc Point and the rock piles tight to Fishers Island are dead calm and empty at midday, then come alive after the sun drops. If you want a daytime striper in Fishers Island Sound right now, you're mostly fishing for a mistake. If you want a real bite, you're fishing dusk through first light.

Eels are doing the work. I've been putting 8- to 10-inch rigged eels on spinning gear and working them slow along the base of the rocks in 8 to 15 feet, right where the boulders drop into the channel edges between Ram Island and the Fishers Island side. No burn on the retrieve — just enough to keep contact and let the current work it. Fish are holding tight to structure, not roaming, so you need to put the eel right on the rock, not near it. Bass to 34 inches came off that pattern this week on the last two hours of the outgoing into the start of the slack, right around 10 p.m.

Here's the piece that's actually helping the eel guys — we just came off the first-quarter neap, and the rip through the Race and down into Fishers Island Sound has gone soft. That current usually rips hard enough to sweep an eel off the structure before it gets down. Right now it's not doing that. The flow is gentle enough that you can hold a presentation right on the rock for longer, work it slower, and cover a piece of structure properly instead of getting one drift and moving on. That window should hold for a few more days before the tides build back toward the full moon, so if you've been frustrated fishing eels through the Race in past weeks because the water moves too fast to control, this is the stretch to try it again.

Daytime, fluke and sea bass are carrying the program, and honestly carrying it well. Fluke fishing on the sand-to-rock transitions inside the Sound has been one of the more dependable things going — drifting white 5-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails over the channel edges in 20 to 35 feet, working the last of the incoming into the top of the tide. Nothing giant, but a lot of keepers in the 18- to 20-inch range, and enough short fish mixed in that you're never bored on the drift. Little Narragansett Bay has been quietly good for this too, especially along the edges where the channel deepens off the flats.

Sea bass on the structure have been the best-kept secret of the week. The rock piles off Watch Hill Reef and the boulder fields on the Fishers Island side are holding good numbers, and the quality's been real — fish in the 3- to 4-pound class on green crab and on 3-inch Gulp on ½-ounce jigs, worked slow and vertical right down into the cracks. That matches what's been coming out of the structure over toward Plum Gut, where a 28-inch, five-pound fish turned heads this past week. Our rock piles are holding the same class of fish. If you're picking bottom, don't be shy about bouncing right on top of the boulders — that's where they're sitting, not off to the side in the sand.

No bonito yet, and I want to be straight about that. We flagged two weeks back that the water was lining up for an early push into the Sound, and it still is — Block Island's holding in the upper 60s, which is right in the window these fish like when they start scouting west. I haven't had a confirmed sighting in Fishers Island Sound yet, and neither has anyone I trust at the dock. But the water's right, the bait's right, and I'd be surprised if we don't start seeing scattered fish working the rips off Watch Hill and around the east end of Fishers Island within the next week or two. Worth having a bag of small epoxy jigs and a 6-weight rigged and ready in the boat just in case you run into a nervous patch of water.

Looking ahead, I'd keep working the eel bite hard through the soft current the next few nights while the neap holds, then expect the rip to tighten back up as we build toward the full moon — that'll mean shorter windows but harder pulls once the tide gets moving again. Daytime, keep drifting the fluke grounds and don't ignore the sea bass on the rock — that's the most consistent meat in the boat right now. And keep one eye on the horizon past Watch Hill. When the bonito show, they won't announce themselves quietly.
